title: Silas and the Drop
premise: Felix Oyelaran, a freelance interpreter who quietly resolves the delegations' ugliest off-record problems, discovers their safe house listed online with interior photos that reveal hidden documents — including proof of who orchestrated the failed peace talks. Hunted by both the broker who leaked the listing and the officials who want the truth buried, Felix must decide whether to trade the documents for safe passage across a border whose checkpoint shifts change at dawn. In the end, Felix gives the secret not to the buyers or the state, but to the delegation's forgotten victims' families, sacrificing their own anonymity and finding, for the first time, a family that chose them back.
about_author: Wren Pemberton is the pen name of a former humanitarian logistics coordinator who spent six years in border towns where paperwork decided who lived. They write thrillers about people whose jobs exist to be denied.

chapters.title: The Language of Deniability
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. We meet Felix mid-negotiation, smoothing over a delegation's threatened collapse in a rain-soaked capital, then returning to the cramped safe house they share with driver Tomas and fixer Ilse — the closest thing to family Felix has had since being disowned for interpreting against their own government. Emotional beat: wary belonging.

chapters.title: Listed
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Scrolling property listings out of boredom, Ilse finds their safe house for sale — with photos showing the interior, including a wall safe and, half-visible, a document folder. Someone is selling their secrets along with the building. Emotional beat: the floor dropping out; home becomes evidence.

chapters.title: What the Camera Saw
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Zooming into the photos, Felix recognizes the folder: testimony naming the minister who sabotaged the peace talks. The listing agent is unreachable; the house was photographed while they slept. Tomas wants to run; Ilse wants to burn it all. Emotional beat: paranoia sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Broker's Open House
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Posing as a buyer, Tomas attends the open house and identifies the 'agent' as Varga, a broker who traffics in leverage, not real estate. Varga knows exactly who Tomas is and offers a trade: the documents for clean exits for all three. Emotional beat: temptation wearing a friendly face.

chapters.title: Shift Change at Kilometer Nine
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Reconnaissance of the border checkpoint reveals the guard rotation changes at dawn — a window when records go unverified. But the route passes through the village where the delegation's massacre survivors live, people Felix has avoided for two years out of shame. Emotional beat: guilt surfacing through geography.

chapters.title: Three Exits, One Door
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Varga escalates: the listing goes public with names attached unless the deal closes by midnight. Ilse discovers Felix has been secretly copying the documents — not to sell, but for something else — and confronts them. Trust fractures. Emotional beat: betrayal that might actually be integrity.

chapters.title: The Families Nobody Billed
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix visits the survivors' cooperative and, through an interpreter they hire instead of speaking directly, offers them the testimony — theirs by right. The families' matriarch asks the question that reframes everything: what will it cost you? Emotional beat: justice redefined as transfer, not transaction.

chapters.title: Midnight Appraisal
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The handoff with Varga goes wrong when his buyers arrive early and armed, planning to take the documents and erase everyone. Tomas stalls them with a fake appraisal while Ilse triggers the safe house's fire alarm, flooding the street with witnesses. Emotional beat: improvised courage under a countdown.

chapters.title: Dawn Rotation
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Climax. With copies already delivered to the families and journalists, Felix walks into the checkpoint carrying nothing but themselves, betting that the truth now public makes them worthless dead and dangerous to detain. Varga's buyers are stopped one lane over, holding an empty folder. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into stillness.

chapters.title: Mother Tongue
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Weeks later, the minister resigns; the families' case proceeds. Felix, unemployable in official circles, interprets for the survivors' cooperative — unpaid, chosen, home. Ilse and Tomas rebuild the safe house into something with a doorbell. Emotional beat: identity no longer defined by secrecy but by who answers when you knock.
